claim: The glutamatergic sensory neurons AWCON and ASH have distinct synaptic dynamics associated with tonic and phasic synaptic properties, respectively.
source: We show that the glutamatergic sensory neurons AWCON and ASH have distinct synaptic dynamics associated with tonic and phasic synaptic properties, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by VGLUT-pHluorin imaging data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Phasic ASH release is strongly dependent on UNC-13.
source: Exocytosis in ASH and AWCON is differentially affected by SNARE-complex regulators that are present in both neurons: phasic ASH release is strongly dependent on UNC-13, whereas tonic AWCON release relies upon UNC-18 and on the protein kinase C homolog PKC-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing ASH neurons had no detectable VGLUT-pH response in unc-13 null mutants (Figure 4B).

claim: Tonic AWCON release relies upon UNC-18.
source: Exocytosis in ASH and AWCON is differentially affected by SNARE-complex regulators that are present in both neurons: phasic ASH release is strongly dependent on UNC-13, whereas tonic AWCON release relies upon UNC-18 and on the protein kinase C homolog PKC-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing AWCON VGLUT-pH responses were nearly eliminated in unc-18 null mutants (Figure 4C).

claim: Tonic AWCON release relies upon the protein kinase C homolog PKC-1.
source: Exocytosis in ASH and AWCON is differentially affected by SNARE-complex regulators that are present in both neurons: phasic ASH release is strongly dependent on UNC-13, whereas tonic AWCON release relies upon UNC-18 and on the protein kinase C homolog PKC-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing pkc-1 mutants had severe defects in VGLUT-pH mobilization in AWCON (Figure 8B,C).

claim: Strong stimuli that elicit high calcium levels increase exocytosis and retrieval rates in AWCON, generating distinct tonic and evoked synaptic modes.
source: Strong stimuli that elicit high calcium levels increase exocytosis and retrieval rates in AWCON, generating distinct tonic and evoked synaptic modes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing AWCON VGLUT-pH retrieval was accelerated during a second odor pulse following elevated calcium (Figure 7B,C).

claim: The AWCON olfactory neurons are tonically active at rest.
source: Based on calcium imaging studies, the AWCON olfactory neurons are tonically active at rest, inhibited (likely hyperpolarized) by odor stimuli, and transiently activated upon odor removal before a return to baseline (Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2014)(Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous calcium imaging studies and by data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: AWCON olfactory neurons are inhibited (likely hyperpolarized) by odor stimuli.
source: Based on calcium imaging studies, the AWCON olfactory neurons are tonically active at rest, inhibited (likely hyperpolarized) by odor stimuli, and transiently activated upon odor removal before a return to baseline (Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2014)(Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous calcium imaging studies and by data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: AWCON olfactory neurons are transiently activated upon odor removal before a return to baseline.
source: Based on calcium imaging studies, the AWCON olfactory neurons are tonically active at rest, inhibited (likely hyperpolarized) by odor stimuli, and transiently activated upon odor removal before a return to baseline (Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2014)(Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous calcium imaging studies and by data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The AWCON signaling pattern resembles that of vertebrate photoreceptors.
source: This pattern resembles that of vertebrate photoreceptors, which employ a similar cGMP sensory transduction cascade (Bargmann, 2006; Zhang and Cote, 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison to known properties of vertebrate photoreceptors, supported by citations.

claim: Vertebrate photoreceptors employ a similar cGMP sensory transduction cascade to AWCON.
source: This pattern resembles that of vertebrate photoreceptors, which employ a similar cGMP sensory transduction cascade (Bargmann, 2006; Zhang and Cote, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on photoreceptor signaling.

claim: ASH nociceptive neurons are strongly activated by noxious chemical and mechanical stimuli.
source: By contrast, calcium imaging and electrophysiological studies of the ASH nociceptive neurons indicate that they are strongly activated by noxious chemical and mechanical stimuli, and recover quickly upon stimulus removal (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2013; Hilliard et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2014)(Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous calcium imaging and electrophysiological studies and by data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: ASH nociceptive neurons recover quickly upon stimulus removal.
source: By contrast, calcium imaging and electrophysiological studies of the ASH nociceptive neurons indicate that they are strongly activated by noxious chemical and mechanical stimuli, and recover quickly upon stimulus removal (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2013; Hilliard et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2014)(Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous calcium imaging and electrophysiological studies and by data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: ASH neurons signal via G protein-regulated TRPV channels.
source: Like vertebrate nociceptive neurons, ASH neurons signal via G protein-regulated TRPV channels (Hilliard et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on ASH signaling mechanisms.

claim: Both AWCON and ASH signal to downstream neurons through glutamatergic synapses and the vesicular glutamate transporter EAT-4.
source: Both AWCON and ASH signal to downstream neurons through glutamatergic synapses and the vesicular glutamate transporter EAT-4 (Chalasani et al., 2007; Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on neurotransmission in these neurons.

claim: The VGLUT-pH reporter was exclusively localized to the axon in both AWCON and ASH.
source: The VGLUT-pH reporter was exclusively localized to the axon in both AWCON and ASH, with a semi-punctate distribution in synaptic regions (Figure 1C, left panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Delivery of butanone to AWCON resulted in a reduction of VGLUT-pH fluorescence with recovery after odor removal.
source: Delivery of butanone to AWCON resulted in a reduction of VGLUT-pH fluorescence with recovery after odor removal (Figure 1C, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Delivery of NaCl to ASH resulted in an increase in VGLUT-pH fluorescence, followed by a decrease after NaCl removal.
source: Delivery of NaCl to ASH resulted in an increase in VGLUT-pH fluorescence, followed by a decrease after NaCl removal (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Over 97% of stimuli triggered a detectable VGLUT-pH response in AWCON and ASH synapses.
source: AWCON and ASH synapses appeared to be highly reliable, as over 97% of stimuli triggered a detectable VGLUT-pH response (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 1E,G.

claim: In ASH, VGLUT-pH fluorescence rose rapidly upon stimulus addition, and fell immediately upon stimulus removal, closely resembling the calcium response.
source: In ASH, VGLUT-pH fluorescence rose rapidly upon stimulus addition, and fell immediately upon stimulus removal, closely resembling the calcium response (Figure 1D,E, compare 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D,E,B.

claim: ASH synaptic vesicle exocytosis is induced by stimulus-triggered calcium entry, and terminates rapidly with subsequent endocytosis and reacidification.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which ASH synaptic vesicle exocytosis is induced by stimulus-triggered calcium entry, and terminates rapidly with subsequent endocytosis and reacidification.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed VGLUT-pH and calcium dynamics in ASH.

claim: pHluorin tethered to the extracellular face of the ASH plasma membrane as a CD4 fusion protein did not respond to NaCl with fluorescence changes.
source: In a control experiment, pHluorin tethered to the extracellular face of the ASH plasma membrane as a CD4 fusion protein did not respond to NaCl with fluorescence changes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that the signal reflects synaptic vesicle dynamics and not changes in extracellular pH.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: The VGLUT-pH signal in ASH reflects synaptic vesicle dynamics and not changes in extracellular pH.
source: In a control experiment, pHluorin tethered to the extracellular face of the ASH plasma membrane as a CD4 fusion protein did not respond to NaCl with fluorescence changes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that the signal reflects synaptic vesicle dynamics and not changes in extracellular pH.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the control experiment with CD4-pH showing no response.

claim: In AWCON, VGLUT-pH fluorescence decreased throughout a one minute odor presentation.
source: In AWCON, VGLUT-pH fluorescence decreased throughout a one minute odor presentation, and odor removal resulted in a rapid increase to pre-stimulus levels without an overshoot (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Odor removal in AWCON resulted in a rapid increase in VGLUT-pH fluorescence to pre-stimulus levels without an overshoot.
source: In AWCON, VGLUT-pH fluorescence decreased throughout a one minute odor presentation, and odor removal resulted in a rapid increase to pre-stimulus levels without an overshoot (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The AWCON neuron has tonic synaptic vesicle release, with basal VGLUT-pH fluorescence determined by steady-state levels of exocytosis versus endocytosis and reacidification.
source: The properties are consistent with a kinetic model in which the AWCON neuron has tonic synaptic vesicle release, with basal VGLUT-pH fluorescence determined by steady-state levels of exocytosis versus endocytosis and reacidification.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed VGLUT-pH dynamics in AWCON.

claim: In AWCON, odor addition reduces calcium and synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
source: In this model, odor addition reduces calcium and synaptic vesicle exocytosis, and odor removal triggers a calcium increase, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, and a return to the pre-stimulus steady state.
evidence: This is part of the kinetic model proposed based on observed dynamics.

claim: In AWCON, odor removal triggers a calcium increase, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, and a return to the pre-stimulus steady state.
source: In this model, odor addition reduces calcium and synaptic vesicle exocytosis, and odor removal triggers a calcium increase, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, and a return to the pre-stimulus steady state.
evidence: This is part of the kinetic model proposed based on observed dynamics.

claim: AWCON fluorescence had an initial fast rate of increase for ~1 s after odor removal, and then transitioned to a slower rate of increase over the following ~5 s.
source: A close examination of VGLUT-pH signals after odor removal showed that AWCON fluorescence had an initial fast rate of increase for ~1 s, and then transitioned to a slower rate of increase over the following ~5 s (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of VGLUT-pH dynamics shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Synaptic vesicle exocytosis is transiently enhanced above its basal level immediately after odor removal in AWCON.
source: These dynamics suggest that synaptic vesicle exocytosis is transiently enhanced above its basal level immediately after odor removal, in agreement with the known calcium overshoot in the AWCON cell body (e.g. Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed dynamics, supported by comparison to calcium imaging data.

claim: Synaptic calcium levels monitored with synaptogyrin-GCaMP rose and fell substantially more quickly than those in the cell body.
source: Synaptic calcium levels monitored with synaptogyrin-GCaMP rose and fell substantially more quickly than those in the cell body (Figure 2C,D; compare Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of synaptic and somatic calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C,D and Figure 1A.

claim: The peak rate of calcium entry in AWCON, at ~1 s after odor removal, occurred at the same time as the peak rate of VGLUT-pH fluorescence increase.
source: The peak rate of calcium entry, at ~1 s after odor removal, occurred at the same time as the peak rate of VGLUT-pH fluorescence increase (Figure 2B,D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal correlation analysis of calcium and VGLUT-pH dynamics shown in Figure 2B,D,G.

claim: Removing odor after a 10 s exposure elicited a small synaptic calcium overshoot within the first second in AWCON.
source: Removing odor after a 10 s exposure elicited a small synaptic calcium overshoot within the first second (Figure 2D,G), and a small increase in exocytosis during the same interval (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by synaptic calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D,G.

claim: Removing odor after a 10 s exposure elicited a small increase in exocytosis during the first second in AWCON.
source: Removing odor after a 10 s exposure elicited a small synaptic calcium overshoot within the first second (Figure 2D,G), and a small increase in exocytosis during the same interval (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by VGLUT-pH imaging data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Both synaptic calcium and exocytosis rates were elevated more substantially for ~1 s after a 60 s or 180 s odor exposure in AWCON.
source: Both synaptic calcium and exocytosis rates were elevated more substantially for ~1 s after a 60 s or 180 s odor exposure (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by synaptic calcium and VGLUT-pH imaging data shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: The transient synaptic calcium overshoot following long odor stimuli evokes a brief pulse of synaptic vesicle release above the tonic level in AWCON.
source: This correspondence suggests that the transient synaptic calcium overshoot following long odor stimuli evokes a brief pulse of synaptic vesicle release above the tonic level.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correspondence between calcium and exocytosis dynamics.

claim: Expressing the light chain of tetanus toxin (TeTx), which cleaves synaptobrevin, in either AWCON or ASH eliminated their VGLUT-pH responses.
source: Expressing the light chain of tetanus toxin (TeTx), which cleaves synaptobrevin (Schiavo et al., 1992), in either AWCON or ASH eliminated their VGLUT-pH responses, as predicted if the VGLUT-pH signals report synaptic vesicle dynamics (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and citation to the mechanism of TeTx.

claim: Tetanus toxin light chain cleaves synaptobrevin.
source: Expressing the light chain of tetanus toxin (TeTx), which cleaves synaptobrevin (Schiavo et al., 1992), in either AWCON or ASH eliminated their VGLUT-pH responses, as predicted if the VGLUT-pH signals report synaptic vesicle dynamics (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: AWCON VGLUT-pH fluorescence did not decrease upon odor addition in TeTx animals.
source: Notably, AWCON VGLUT-pH fluorescence did not decrease upon odor addition in TeTx animals, suggesting that both tonic AWCON exocytosis and the evoked exocytosis after long odor stimuli require the SNARE complex.
evidence: This observation is based on experimental data with TeTx expression.

claim: Both tonic AWCON exocytosis and the evoked exocytosis after long odor stimuli require the SNARE complex.
source: Notably, AWCON VGLUT-pH fluorescence did not decrease upon odor addition in TeTx animals, suggesting that both tonic AWCON exocytosis and the evoked exocytosis after long odor stimuli require the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the TeTx experimental results.

claim: unc-64(e246) syntaxin mutants had diminished VGLUT-pH responses in AWCON and ASH.
source: Both unc-64(e246) (Figure 3C,D) and ric-4(md1088) (Figure 3E,F) had diminished VGLUT-pH responses in AWCON and ASH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: ric-4(md1088) SNAP-25 mutants had diminished VGLUT-pH responses in AWCON and ASH.
source: Both unc-64(e246) (Figure 3C,D) and ric-4(md1088) (Figure 3E,F) had diminished VGLUT-pH responses in AWCON and ASH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The results with unc-64 and ric-4 mutants are consistent with a requirement for the SNARE complex in tonic and evoked glutamate release from AWCON and evoked glutamate release from ASH.
source: These results are consistent with a requirement for the SNARE complex in tonic and evoked glutamate release from AWCON and evoked glutamate release from ASH.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mutant analysis results.

claim: ASH neurons had no detectable VGLUT-pH response to sensory stimuli in unc-13 null mutants.
source: ASH neurons had no detectable VGLUT-pH response to sensory stimuli in unc-13 null mutants, indicating an absolute requirement for this protein in ASH synaptic vesicle mobilization (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: UNC-13 is absolutely required for ASH synaptic vesicle mobilization.
source: ASH neurons had no detectable VGLUT-pH response to sensory stimuli in unc-13 null mutants, indicating an absolute requirement for this protein in ASH synaptic vesicle mobilization (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complete absence of response in unc-13 null mutants.

claim: AWCON neurons in unc-13 null mutants had a significant, albeit reduced, increase in VGLUT-pH signal after odor removal indicative of residual synaptic activity.
source: By contrast, AWCON neurons in unc-13 null mutants had a significant, albeit reduced, increase in VGLUT-pH signal after odor removal indicative of residual synaptic activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AWCON VGLUT-pH responses were nearly eliminated in unc-18 null mutants.
source: AWCON VGLUT-pH responses were nearly eliminated in unc-18 null mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: unc-18 ASH neurons responded to stimuli by mobilizing VGLUT-pH, albeit to a lesser extent than the wild-type.
source: However, unc-18 ASH neurons responded to stimuli by mobilizing VGLUT-pH, albeit to a lesser extent than the wild-type (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ASH has a stronger requirement for unc-13 and a weaker requirement for unc-18 than AWCON.
source: These results reveal heterogeneity in the requirements for SNARE regulators in different cell types: ASH has a stronger requirement for unc-13 and a weaker requirement for unc-18 than AWCON (Statistics in Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the differential effects of unc-13 and unc-18 mutations in the two cell types.

claim: Synaptic vesicle release was reduced but not eliminated in both ASH and AWCON neurons by mutations affecting the scaffold protein UNC-10/RIM.
source: Synaptic vesicle release was reduced but not eliminated in both ASH and AWCON neurons by mutations affecting the scaffold protein UNC-10/RIM (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: ASH neurons showed enhanced synaptic vesicle release in cpx-1/complexin mutants.
source: ASH neurons showed enhanced synaptic vesicle release in mutations for the SNARE regulator cpx-1/complexin mutants (Figure 4H); a similar trend in AWCON was not statistically significant (Figure 4G, Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Expressing an untagged super-ecliptic pHluorin in the cytoplasm of AWCON and ASH neurons (cyto-pH) reported robust stimulus-dependent pH changes.
source: Similarly, expressing an untagged super-ecliptic pHluorin in the cytoplasm of AWCON and ASH neurons (cyto-pH) reported robust stimulus-dependent pH changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations with cytoplasmic pHluorin.

claim: Odor addition increased cyto-pH fluorescence in AWCON, suggesting alkalinization.
source: Odor addition increased cyto-pH fluorescence in AWCON, suggesting alkalinization, and odor removal decreased cyto-pH fluorescence, suggesting activity-dependent acidification (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytoplasmic pH imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Odor removal decreased cyto-pH fluorescence in AWCON, suggesting activity-dependent acidification.
source: Odor addition increased cyto-pH fluorescence in AWCON, suggesting alkalinization, and odor removal decreased cyto-pH fluorescence, suggesting activity-dependent acidification (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytoplasmic pH imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: AWCON cytoplasmic pH changes were opposite in sign to the signals detected by VGLUT-pH.
source: These pH changes were opposite in sign to the signals defected by VGLUT-pH (compare Figure 5A to 1G), and were strongest in the axon, intermediate in the cell body, and weak in the sensory dendrite (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of cytoplasmic pH and VGLUT-pH data.

claim: AWCON cytoplasmic pH changes were strongest in the axon, intermediate in the cell body, and weak in the sensory dendrite.
source: These pH changes were opposite in sign to the signals defected by VGLUT-pH (compare Figure 5A to 1G), and were strongest in the axon, intermediate in the cell body, and weak in the sensory dendrite (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular analysis of cytoplasmic pH changes shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In ASH, NaCl stimuli elicited a decrease in cyto-pH fluorescence suggestive of acidification.
source: In ASH, NaCl stimuli elicited a decrease in cyto-pH fluorescence suggestive of acidification, again the opposite sign of the VGLUT-pH signal (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytoplasmic pH imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ASH cytoplasmic pH changes were opposite in sign to the VGLUT-pH signal.
source: In ASH, NaCl stimuli elicited a decrease in cyto-pH fluorescence suggestive of acidification, again the opposite sign of the VGLUT-pH signal (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of cytoplasmic pH and VGLUT-pH data.

claim: AWCON cyto-pH signals were normal in unc-13 or unc-18 mutations.
source: Unlike VGLUT-pH responses, AWCON cyto-pH signals were normal in unc-13 or unc-18 mutations (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Cytoplasmic pH changes are independent of synaptic vesicle release.
source: These results suggest that cytoplasmic pH changes are independent of synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that cyto-pH signals are normal in synaptic mutants.

claim: A large fraction of AWCON traces were consistent with single exponential decay, with an 18 s time constant.
source: A large fraction of traces were consistent with single exponential decay, with an 18 s time constant for AWCON and an 8 s time constant for ASH (Figure 6C,D); a subset of traces were consistent with double exponential decay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by exponential fitting analysis shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: A large fraction of ASH traces were consistent with single exponential decay, with an 8 s time constant.
source: A large fraction of traces were consistent with single exponential decay, with an 18 s time constant for AWCON and an 8 s time constant for ASH (Figure 6C,D); a subset of traces were consistent with double exponential decay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by exponential fitting analysis shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: A subset of AWCON and ASH traces were consistent with double exponential decay.
source: A large fraction of traces were consistent with single exponential decay, with an 18 s time constant for AWCON and an 8 s time constant for ASH (Figure 6C,D); a subset of traces were consistent with double exponential decay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by exponential fitting analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The measured decay constants within and between neurons did not correlate with axon fluorescence before endocytosis.
source: The measured decay constants within and between neurons did not correlate with axon fluorescence before endocytosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that VGLUT-pH expression levels did not saturate the endocytosis machinery (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: VGLUT-pH expression levels did not saturate the endocytosis machinery.
source: The measured decay constants within and between neurons did not correlate with axon fluorescence before endocytosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that VGLUT-pH expression levels did not saturate the endocytosis machinery (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of correlation between expression levels and decay constants, supported by citation.

claim: In AWCON neurons upon odor addition, and in ASH neurons after stimulus removal, unc-11(e47) null mutants had significantly slowed VGLUT-pH retrieval.
source: Indeed, in AWCON neurons upon odor addition, and in ASH neurons after stimulus removal, unc-11(e47) null mutants had significantly slowed VGLUT-pH retrieval (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–H.

claim: Exocytosis may also be impacted in unc-11(e47) mutants, as a significant fraction of trials produced weak or undetectable responses in ASH.
source: Exocytosis may also be impacted in unc-11(e47) mutants, as a significant fraction of trials produced weak or undetectable responses in ASH (Figure 6F, gray trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Baseline VGLUT-pH fluorescence was higher in unc-11(e47) mutants than in wild-type for both neurons.
source: Baseline VGLUT-pH fluorescence was higher in unc-11(e47) mutants than in wild-type for both neurons, consistent with increased VGLUT-pH on the cell surface or in other neutral compartments (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I,J.

claim: The increased baseline VGLUT-pH fluorescence in unc-11(e47) mutants is consistent with increased VGLUT-pH on the cell surface or in other neutral compartments.
source: Baseline VGLUT-pH fluorescence was higher in unc-11(e47) mutants than in wild-type for both neurons, consistent with increased VGLUT-pH on the cell surface or in other neutral compartments (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the increased baseline fluorescence observation.

claim: Endocytosis in other systems is accelerated at high calcium concentrations.
source: This difference in calcium levels could affect vesicle traffic, as endocytosis in other systems is accelerated at high calcium concentrations (Leitz and Kavalali, 2016; Neves et al., 2001; Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge from other systems, supported by citations.

claim: AWCON VGLUT-pH retrieval was accelerated during the second odor pulse, matching the ~8 s retrieval time observed in ASH.
source: Strikingly, AWCON VGLUT-pH retrieval was accelerated during the second odor pulse, matching the ~8 s retrieval time observed in ASH (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The acceleration effect in AWCON endocytosis was temporary (lasting <70 s) but could be induced again after another 60 s odor pulse.
source: The effect was temporary (lasting <70 s) but could be induced again after another 60 s odor pulse (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: unc-11(e47) mutants were also regulated by the dual odor-pulse protocol, and delayed compared to wild-type under both conditions.
source: unc-11(e47) mutants were also regulated by the dual odor-pulse protocol, and delayed compared to wild-type under both conditions (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: VGLUT-pH retrieval in AWCON is regulated by activity, consistent with calcium-dependent acceleration of endocytosis.
source: These results indicate that VGLUT-pH retrieval in AWCON is regulated by activity, consistent with calcium-dependent acceleration of endocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed activity-dependent changes in retrieval kinetics.

claim: pkc-1 is required for normal behavioral responses to odors detected by AWCON.
source: pkc-1 is required for normal behavioral responses to odors detected by AWCON, and has previously been suggested to act at a step downstream of AWCON calcium entry (Tsunozaki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: pkc-1 has previously been suggested to act at a step downstream of AWCON calcium entry.
source: pkc-1 is required for normal behavioral responses to odors detected by AWCON, and has previously been suggested to act at a step downstream of AWCON calcium entry (Tsunozaki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a previous hypothesis from cited work.

claim: Calcium response to odor stimulation is normal in pkc-1 mutants.
source: We confirmed the normal calcium response to odor stimulation in pkc-1 mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B), and additionally determined that synaptic calcium signals detected with synaptogyrin-GCaMP were normal or slightly increased in pkc-1 mutants (Figure 8A,B, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Synaptic calcium signals detected with synaptogyrin-GCaMP were normal or slightly increased in pkc-1 mutants.
source: We confirmed the normal calcium response to odor stimulation in pkc-1 mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B), and additionally determined that synaptic calcium signals detected with synaptogyrin-GCaMP were normal or slightly increased in pkc-1 mutants (Figure 8A,B, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by synaptic calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: VGLUT-pH signals in mutants with the kinase-inactivating mutation pkc-1(nj1) were severely diminished across all conditions.
source: By contrast, VGLUT-pH signals in mutants with the kinase-inactivating mutation pkc-1(nj1) were severely diminished across all conditions, resembling those of strong SNARE mutants (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Three additional pkc-1 alleles had related defects: in each case, the response to odor addition was nearly eliminated, and the response to odor removal was diminished to a greater or lesser degree.
source: Three additional pkc-1 alleles had related defects: in each case, the response to odor addition was nearly eliminated, and the response to odor removal was diminished to a greater or lesser degree (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Selective transgenic expression of a pkc-1 cDNA in AWCON resulted in full rescue of the VGLUT-pH defect and the behavioral defect.
source: Selective transgenic expression of a pkc-1 cDNA in AWCON resulted in full rescue of the VGLUT-pH defect and the behavioral defect (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), indicating that pkc-1 affects synaptic vesicle exocytosis cell autonomously in AWCON.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: pkc-1 affects synaptic vesicle exocytosis cell autonomously in AWCON.
source: Selective transgenic expression of a pkc-1 cDNA in AWCON resulted in full rescue of the VGLUT-pH defect and the behavioral defect (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), indicating that pkc-1 affects synaptic vesicle exocytosis cell autonomously in AWCON.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell-specific rescue experiment.

claim: VGLUT-pH signals in ASH neurons were only slightly affected by pkc-1.
source: In contrast with AWCON, VGLUT-pH signals in ASH neurons were only slightly affected by pkc-1: pkc-1 mutants substantially preserved both exocytosis and retrieval dynamics in ASH (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E–G.

claim: pkc-1 mutants substantially preserved both exocytosis and retrieval dynamics in ASH.
source: In contrast with AWCON, VGLUT-pH signals in ASH neurons were only slightly affected by pkc-1: pkc-1 mutants substantially preserved both exocytosis and retrieval dynamics in ASH (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E–G.

claim: A subtle pkc-1 defect was observed upon repetitive stimulation in ASH, where VGLUT-pH exocytosis responses were diminished compared to wild-type.
